# Heatmaps {#sec-heatmaps} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## Theme: `theme_freshprince()` Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_freshprince()`, modeled on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air logo: a pink glow background, a graffiti green frame and title, green, teal, lime, and olive marks, and an Arial Black title. Continuous fills run from teal to lime. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ two numeric (continuous) variables** **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](heatmaps_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: :::: ## Description A heatmap is made of colored boxes set out in rows and columns,[^matrix] where the color of each box stands for a number. Heatmaps put groups[^categories] on the `x` and `y` axes, and each box is where a group on the `x` axis meets a group on the `y` axis. The color of each box[^cell] comes from its number. Heatmaps are good at showing how big[^magnitude] numbers are across two sets of groups,[^dimensions] and they often come with a key that shows which color goes with which number.[^color-scale] How strong the color is[^saturation] changes from box to box to show the number where two groups meet. Put the key above or below a heatmap, and run it from left to right.[^legend-position] That keeps the form of the heatmap and makes it easier to read. ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation library(tidyr) # for expand_grid() ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: *The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air* was a funny show about a young man named Will who goes to live with his rich family. It ran for six seasons (1990 to 1996). A running gag is a funny bit that a show does again and again, and this show had a few of them. We'll make up[^simulate] whether each gag shows up in each of the 24 episodes in a season. Every gag gets a starting chance of showing up (`base`) and a `trend` that makes it show up more or less often as the show goes on. `plogis()` turns those numbers into a chance between 0 and 1,[^probability] and `rbinom()` uses that chance to pick yes or no for every gag in every episode[^weighted-coin] (`present` is 1 when the gag shows up). Then we add up the episodes that have each gag in each season (`occurrences`). Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 144 episodes every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1990) # same episodes every time the code runs fp_gags <- tibble( gag = c("Will flirts", "Phil yells at Will", "Geoffrey zinger", # six running gags "Jazz thrown out", "Hilary goes shopping", "Carlton dance"), base = c(1.5, 1.2, 0.8, -0.4, -0.2, -2.2), # how common each gag is (higher is more common) trend = c(-0.3, -0.1, 0, 0.2, 0, 0.5) # change per season (positive gags grow) ) fp_episodes <- fp_gags |> tidyr::expand_grid(season = 1:6, episode = 1:24) |> # every gag in every episode mutate( p = plogis(base + trend * (season - 3.5)), # chance the gag shows up in that episode present = rbinom(n(), size = 1, prob = p) # 1 = the gag happened, 0 = it didn't ) fp_heatmap <- fp_episodes |> group_by(season, gag) |> # one group per gag per season summarise(occurrences = sum(present), .groups = "drop") # episodes with the gag glimpse(fp_heatmap) #> Rows: 36 #> Columns: 3 #> $ season 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2… #> $ gag "Carlton dance", "Geoffrey z… #> $ occurrences 1, 18, 7, 8, 20, 22, 0, 17, … ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution Every box in a heatmap is a number, and every number here comes from adding up 24 yes or no choices.[^outcomes] A gag that shows up in most episodes gives light boxes in every season, and a gag whose chances grow over time gives boxes that get lighter from left to right. Below we'll move from the episodes, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula] ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first four episodes of season 1. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} fp_episodes |> filter(season == 1, episode <= 4) |> select(gag, episode, p, present) |> arrange(episode) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: Each row is one yes or no choice, and `p` is the chance it comes out 1. When Will flirts, he tries to get a girl to like him. Carlton is a young man in Will's rich family. Will flirts in almost every episode (`p` is above 0.9), while the Carlton dance has only about a 3% chance in season 1. Now look at how many episodes have each of those two gags in each of the six seasons, next to the numbers we'd expect[^expected] (24 episodes times `p`). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} fp_episodes |> filter(gag %in% c("Will flirts", "Carlton dance")) |> group_by(gag, season) |> summarise(occurrences = sum(present), expected = round(24 * first(p), 1), .groups = "drop") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: The Carlton dance goes from almost never to a few times a season, while Will flirts in nearly every episode, no matter the season. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: Below are two heatmaps. The first shows the numbers we'd expect (24 times `p`), and the second shows what our made up data really gave us. The two look much the same: Will's flirting stays light in every season, and the Carlton dance gets lighter, a little at a time, from left to right. The made up heatmap changes more from box to box, because each box is only 24 yes or no choices. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} fp_episodes |> distinct(gag, season, p) |> ggplot(aes(x = season, y = gag, fill = 24 * p)) + geom_tile() + scale_fill_continuous(limits = c(0, 24)) + labs(title = "Expected", x = "Season", y = NULL, fill = "Episodes") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ggplot(fp_heatmap, aes(x = season, y = gag, fill = occurrences)) + geom_tile() + scale_fill_continuous(limits = c(0, 24)) + labs(title = "Simulated", x = "Season", y = NULL, fill = "Episodes") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](heatmaps_files/figure-html/draw_heatmap-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](heatmaps_files/figure-html/draw_heatmap-2.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: Each gag in each episode is [one yes or no choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_trial)[^bernoulli] with a chance of $p$. Adding up 24 of these choices, where no choice changes any other,[^independent] gives us [the rule for how many times out of 24 we get a yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution):[^binomial] $$ \text{occurrences} \sim \text{Binomial}(n = 24, \; p_{\text{gag, season}}) $$ The number we'd expect is $24p$, and how far the numbers usually fall from it[^sd] is $\sqrt{24p(1 - p)}$. This number is biggest when $p = 0.5$ (about 2.4 episodes) and gets close to 0 when a gag almost always or almost never shows up. That's why the Will flirts row looks so much the same from season to season, while the middle rows change a lot from one season to the next. The chance itself comes from `plogis()`, which turns `base + trend * (season - 3.5)` into a number between 0 and 1. A `trend` above 0 (like the 0.5 for the Carlton dance) makes a gag more likely every season. Jazz is Will's friend, and in one gag he gets thrown out of the house. Try giving "Jazz thrown out" a `trend` below 0 and watch his row get darker from left to right. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()` - Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data` - Put `season` on the `x` axis, `gag` on the `y` axis, and `occurrences` in the color of each box[^fill] - Add `geom_tile()` on top[^layer] - Move the key below the graph with `theme(legend.position = "bottom")` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_heatmap_tile <- labs( title = "The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Running gags per season (24 episodes each)", x = "Season", y = "Running gag", fill = "Episodes") ggp2_heatmap_tile <- ggplot(data = fp_heatmap, aes(x = season, y = gag, fill = occurrences)) + geom_tile() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ggp2_heatmap_tile + labs_heatmap_tile ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](heatmaps_files/figure-html/create_graph_heatmap-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ## More info Along with `geom_tile()`, we can make heatmaps with `geom_raster()`. ### `geom_raster()`
- Make the words around the graph[^labels-raster] with `labs()` - Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data` - Put `season` on the `x` axis, `gag` on the `y` axis, and `occurrences` in the color of each box[^fill-raster] - Add `geom_raster()` on top[^layer-raster] - Move the key below the graph with `theme(legend.position = "bottom")` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} labs_heatmap_raster <- labs( title = "The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Running gags per season (24 episodes each)", x = "Season", y = "Running gag", fill = "Episodes") ggp2_heatmap_raster <- ggplot(data = fp_heatmap, aes(x = season, y = gag, fill = occurrences)) + geom_raster() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ggp2_heatmap_raster + labs_heatmap_raster ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](heatmaps_files/figure-html/code_graph_raster-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: [^matrix]: A matrix. [^categories]: Categories (categorical variables). [^cell]: A cell. `geom_tile()` draws each cell as a tile. [^magnitude]: Magnitude. [^dimensions]: Two dimensions. [^color-scale]: A color scale, shown in the legend. [^saturation]: Color saturation (the grade of purity or vividness). [^legend-position]: Position the legend on top or bottom and justify it horizontally to preserve the shape of the heatmap and improve readability. [^packages]: Install and load the packages. [^simulate]: Simulate. [^probability]: A probability. `plogis()` is the logistic (inverse logit) function. [^weighted-coin]: `rbinom()` with `size = 1` flips a weighted coin (one Bernoulli draw) for every gag in every episode. [^seed]: Setting the random seed. [^outcomes]: Each tile is a count of 24 binary (yes or no) outcomes. [^formula]: The formula. [^expected]: The expected counts, $24p$. [^bernoulli]: A Bernoulli trial: a single yes or no outcome with probability $p$. [^independent]: Independent trials. [^binomial]: A binomial distribution. [^sd]: The standard deviation, a measure of spread. [^labels]: The labels (title, subtitle, caption, axis titles, and legend title). [^fill]: Map `occurrences` to the `fill` aesthetic. [^layer]: Add the `geom_tile()` layer. [^labels-raster]: The labels (title, subtitle, caption, axis titles, and legend title). [^fill-raster]: Map `occurrences` to the `fill` aesthetic. [^layer-raster]: Add the `geom_raster()` layer.
